title: Check the firm before you invest, FCA warns, as AI scams rise
summary: A third (33%) of UK adults say they have seen an investment promotion in the past year that they believe used artificial intelligence (AI), new research from the FCA shows. Reports of investment fraud to Report Fraud that mention suspected use of AI have risen by nearly 400% in a year, up from 193 in 2024/25 to 956 in 2025/26. Investment fraud victims lost an average of £28,188 in 2025/26.Most people feel confident they could spot an AI investment scam, but that confidence is lower when a well-known person is involved. Almost two-thirds (62%) of adults say they could identify an investment scam that used AI. But less than half (49%) think they could tell whether a video or voice recording of a well-known person had been generated or altered by AI.Martin Lewis was the person most often named by those who thought they had seen a fake promotion featuring a well-known person.Under-35s are the most confident and the most exposed. Around three-quarters (74%) say they could identify an AI investment scam, and more than half (56%) believe they have seen an AI-generated investment promotion in the past year. title: Motor finance compensation scheme calculation
summary: While preparing our response to the legal challenges to our motor finance redress scheme, we identified some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements. This data informed the annual percentage rate (APR) adjustment we use in our calculation of compensation. We set this at 17% for agreements from 1 April 2014. Our initial work to understand the impact of the errors suggests that, if there is any impact, this would be less than 1 percentage point either side of 17%.While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation.We properly informed those challenging the scheme. Two of those challengers are due to serve their expert evidence on Friday 27 November 2026. We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation.We are sorry for the further uncertainty this creates for consumers and firms. title: ES - 2026-11-26 - Jan Camenisch, Julien Donnet, Simon Lavater and Thomas Moser: Wholesale CBDC on public permissionless blockchains: Challenges, trade-offs, and design choices
summary: Stablecoins are the dominant settlement asset on public permissionless blockchains, but as private money they expose users to credit and liquidity risk and can trade away from par. Wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) offers settlement in central bank money, free of credit risk, but has so far been implemented only on permissioned platforms. This paper examines the feasibility of issuing wCBDC on public permissionless blockchains, where tokenized financial activity is growing. It does not advocate such a step. Rather, it analyzes the safeguards such a design would require, focusing on direct Layer-1 issuance as the case in which the central bank has the least control over the underlying infrastructure. The analysis shows that central bank control differs across three levels. At the asset level, smart-contract rules allow the central bank to retain control over the monetary instrument. At the application level, interaction with third-party smart contracts enables composability but complicates eligibility controls and orderly exit.
